pixels.lens: Pixels and instrument. Is this a real point source at a fixed place on the sky, and is it measured correctly? I used my own astropy, numpy and scipy code on the 370 cached SPHEREx cutouts (all six detectors, three visits). I did not call backend/photometry.py or backend/sweep.py.

findings.what: WEAKENS the sweep's numbers: the Aug-Sep 2025 'faint state' (D6 24, D5 39, D4 38, D3 27 mJy) is not light from the candidate. It is light from neighbouring stars inside the 15-arcsec aperture. My aperture sums match the sweep's figures. A PSF fit at the source's own place, with the catalogued neighbours held at their positions, finds almost nothing. The candidate was undetected in Aug-Sep 2025 (at most about 2 mJy, which is the level of the faint catalogued stars 3.7-4.8 arcsec away). The real rise is therefore at least about 400 times, not 35 times. It switched on between 2025-09-15 and 2026-02-26: it did not 'rise steadily through 2025'.
findings.evidence: out/forced_table.json and analyse2.py output (pass 3, WCS corrected). Aug-Sep 2025 forced PSF flux at the bright place: D6 0.28 mJy (12 clean exposures), D5 1.16 (18), D4 0.79 (13), D3 0.43 (14). For comparison, 12 empty control places per exposure give medians of -1.0 to -1.3 mJy, with a per-exposure robust scatter of 0.75 to 1.2 mJy. In the same exposures the catalogued star 2MASS J16524412-4440318 / CWISE J165244.11-444031.9 (W2 9.05, 10 arcsec to the northeast) is fitted at 33-46 mJy. Ratio of 1.5-px to 2.5-px aperture flux: 0.35 in D6 Aug 2025, against 0.84-0.86 when bright, so the light was not centred on the place. Randomly placed 2.5-px apertures in this field give a median of +12 to +17 mJy with a scatter of 20-27 mJy in D4-D6, so the sweep's faint values sit within 1 sigma of a random aperture. D5 forced flux on 2025-09-14/15 is 1.1, 1.2 and 1.7 mJy: no rise inside the first visit.

findings.what: WEAKENS the sweep's counterpart: the light does not fall on the catalogued faint star. It sits 3.7-4.9 arcsec from every catalogued object, between a GLIMPSE source 3.7 arcsec to the west-northwest and the CatWISE/2MASS/Gaia star 3.7-4.9 arcsec to the east. With SPHEREx centroids good to about 0.3 arcsec, that offset is real (more than 10 sigma). The faint red star the sweep calls the counterpart is a neighbour, and the source that brightened is not in any of Gaia DR3, 2MASS, GLIMPSE, AllWISE or CatWISE2020.
findings.evidence: out/centroids.json and out/catalogue_offsets.json. Mean of 93 bright exposures (D4, D5, D6) with the zero point taken from field stars: east -0.198 ± 0.026, north -0.275 ± 0.023 arcsec from the sweep's place (scatter 0.25 and 0.22 per exposure). A single Gaussian fitted without neighbours moves it by 0.25 arcsec; Mar against Aug 2026 differ by 0.29 arcsec. Distances from the bright place: CatWISE J165243.63-444036.8 (W2 13.34, error 0.08 arcsec) 3.66 arcsec, 3.65 to the east; GLIMPSE G341.0882-00.4146 ([3.6] 14.24) 3.68, to the west-northwest; GLIMPSE G341.0893-00.4165 ([4.5] 12.47) 4.45; 2MASS J16524373-4440366 (Ks 13.77) 4.81; Gaia DR3 5964332607636528768 (G 19.35, BP-RP 3.60, motion -1.9/-2.2 mas/yr) 4.93; CatWISE J165242.75-444036.4 5.69. Field-star zero points per detector are -0.06 to -0.28 arcsec (6 to 12 stars per exposure).

findings.what: WEAKENS the D3 figures and limits the flux precision: the sweep's D3 values (27, 86, 53) are mostly neighbour light. The source's own D3 flux is 0.4, 25 and 7.7 mJy. In Aug 2026 the D4 core is saturated (BLOOM, or OVERFLOW plus SUR_ERROR) in 7 of 18 exposures, which give only lower limits of 380-618 mJy at 3.3-3.8 um. Every clean D5 and D6 reading in Aug 2026 carries OVERFLOW on its core pixels. Those are valid partial reads under the Explanatory Supplement, but they scatter by 6-10%.
findings.evidence: forced_table.json: D3 0.43 / 25.2 / 7.65 mJy against 2.5-px apertures of 28.0 / 86.6 / 54.4. Core flags in Aug 2026 (pass3): D5 OVERFLOW in 32 of 32, D6 in 18 of 18, with no SUR_ERROR or BLOOM. D4: OVERFLOW 15, BLOOM 5. Saturated D4 raw sums: 2026W34_1A_0591_1/3/4, 2026W35_1A_0056_1 and 0360_1 give 380-618 mJy. D6 Aug 2026 forced flux: 1089, robust scatter 66 mJy.

findings.what: NEUTRAL, a trap found along the way: the archive's sky coordinates (WCS) for exposure 2026W10_1A_0572_4 D5 are off by 2.8 pixels (about 17 arcsec). Measured at the archive's coordinates, the source seems to disappear there (2.7 mJy). After the field-star correction it reads 90.6 mJy, in line with exposures hours either side (80-138).
findings.evidence: out/wcscheck.json: dx -2.14, dy +1.77 px, 14 of 17 stars agree. The header still says FINAST 0 and L2DQAFLG Pass. A second exposure, 2025W34_2B_0043_2 D5, is off by 0.8 px. I applied all coherent shifts in pass 3.

findings.what: SUPPORTS: the source stays at one place on the sky in every detector and visit, with no drift that a moving body or a changing blend would produce.
findings.evidence: Offsets from the adopted place (median, then scatter, arcsec, east and north): D4 Aug 2026 +0.01/-0.07 (0.30/0.27, n=18); D5 Mar 2026 +0.10/+0.02 (0.17/0.12, n=17); D5 Aug 2026 +0.00/+0.11 (0.14/0.17, n=32); D6 Mar 2026 +0.18/-0.23 (n=18); D6 Aug 2026 -0.21/+0.05 (0.16/0.21, n=18); D4 Mar 2026 -0.12/-0.24 (n=18); D3 Mar 2026 -0.13/-0.43 (n=15). Drift within a visit: Mar 2026 +0.11 east / -0.27 north arcsec over 12.1 days; Aug 2026 +0.29 / 0.00 arcsec over 17.2 days. The Aug 2025 free fit wanders to the W2 9.05 star at +8.4 to +8.8 east, +5.1 north, because nothing is at the place.

findings.what: SUPPORTS: the instrument cannot fake it. Between Mar 2026 and Aug 2026 the detector is rotated by 180 degrees and the source falls all over each array, yet it keeps one sky place. Aug 2025 and Aug 2026 have identical pointing geometry, yet the source is absent in one and bright in the other. That rules out persistence, a fixed defect, a fixed-offset ghost or a point-reflected ghost of any of the 85 bright stars within 0.5 degrees.
findings.evidence: out/geometry.json. Detector orientation: Aug 2025 and Aug 2026 185-191 degrees, Mar 2026 6.6-9.3 degrees. Source position on the detector spans x 73-2002 and y 46-2016 across exposures. Only 0-2 pairs of exposures per detector put it within 3 px of the same pixel. The brightest infrared star (AllWISE J165224.64-441253.1, W2 -0.88, 0.465 degrees away) sits at (-74, -263) px from the source in Aug 2025 and Aug 2026 and at (+72, +261) px in Mar 2026. The nearest very bright star (2MASS J16523780-4445419, Ks 3.62, 5.2 arcmin away) sits at (-2, +50) px and then (+2, -50) px. Same-geometry pairs 124-127 px apart: D6 2025W34_2B_0042_1 reads 0.4 mJy against 2026W33_2A_0055_3 at 1014; D5 2025W38_1A_0113_1 1.3 against 2026W33_2A_0152_2 707; D4 2025W34_2B_0364_1 -0.5 against 2026W35_1A_0299_1 240. For all 85 bright stars, the star-minus-source vector on the detector spreads by 100-590 px and the star-plus-source vector by 4,600-5,500 px. No GHOST bit is set within 3 px in any exposure, but the archive never sets those bits, so this proves nothing.

findings.what: SUPPORTS: it is shaped like a star. Width and roundness match field stars of similar brightness fitted with the same model in the same exposures.
findings.evidence: out/shape.json and analyse_shape.py, target against comparison stars within a factor of 2.5 in flux. FWHM (arcsec): D5 Mar 2026 7.38 against 7.38 (96 star fits); D6 Mar 2026 8.64 against 8.17; D4 Aug 2026 8.00 against 8.07; D5 Aug 2026 8.64 against 7.90; D6 Aug 2026 9.43 against 8.52. Field-star FWHM grows with flux (D6: 7.39 at 30-100 mJy, 8.11 at 100-300, 8.52 at 300-1000), so the small excess at about 900 mJy is in line. Axis ratio 0.92-0.96 against 0.92-0.95. Concentration (1.5/2.5 px) 0.78-0.86 against 0.86-0.89; the lower value comes from the 10-arcsec neighbour. In D3 the stack shows the source merged with the 20 mJy neighbour (axis ratio 0.5).

findings.what: SUPPORTS: detectors that share an exposure agree at the same instant, and four separate arrays see the same rise at the same place.
findings.evidence: Same-exposure pairs. D3 with D6 in Mar 2026 (13): D3 3.6-46 mJy alongside D6 254-476; on 03-08, D3 2.31-2.36 um 45-46 with D6 254-288; on 03-15, D3 1.65-1.68 um 3.6-5.1 with D6 326-328. D3 with D6 in Aug 2026 (12): D3 rises smoothly from 2.7 mJy at 1.78 um to 48 at 2.40, with D6 884-1172. D2 with D5 in Mar 2026: D2 1-4 mJy at 1.37-1.62 um alongside D5 80-310. D1 is near 0 (±0.1 mJy) in every visit, as expected for a source this cool.

findings.what: SUPPORTS: the spectrum is a smooth thermal continuum, which an artefact would not give. Aug 2026 fits a single blackbody of about 567 K from 1.6 to 5 um. Mar 2026 is not a single blackbody: the source was rising about 10% per day while the different detectors were observing, it shows near-infrared excess light, and there is a broad dip at 2.8-3.5 um that could be water ice (not established). There are no CO2 (4.27 um) or CO (4.67 um) residuals above about 5% in Aug 2026.
findings.evidence: out/sed_fits.json and pictures/spectrum_by_visit.png, using my forced fluxes and a 10% per-point floor. Aug 2026, D2-D6, 95 points: plain blackbody T = 560 ± 6 K, chi2/dof 59/93. With a time term: T = 567 ± 6 K, F(4.6) = 993 mJy, -1.6 ± 0.4 % per day, chi2/dof 38.7/92. D3-D6 only: 567 K, chi2/dof 35/67. Adding extinction gives T 654 ± 78 K with A_K 1.5 ± 1.2 (degenerate). Mar 2026: plain blackbody chi2/dof 9.2. With a time term: T = 771 ± 14 K, +10.8 ± 0.6 % per day, chi2/dof 2.6. Two blackbodies: chi2/dof 2.96. Residuals: +121% at 2.4-2.8 um, -25% at 2.85-3.8 um. Within D4 (Feb 26 to Mar 2) the flux falls from 49 mJy at 2.42 um to 23 at 3.0 and climbs to 72 at 3.76. Same-wavelength rise: 4.28 um 80 to 171 mJy (03-04 to 03-07), 4.9 um 254 to 476 (03-08 to 03-16). D2 in Aug 2026 (0.3 mJy) is at the level of the 2MASS star 4.8 arcsec away.

findings.what: SUPPORTS: the pictures, which I looked at. In the D6 and D5 stacks a new point source appears at the centre in Mar 2026 and is brighter in Aug 2026; in Aug-Sep 2025 only the 41 mJy neighbour 10 arcsec northeast is there. Every single D6 exposure in Mar and Aug 2026 shows it at the same spot, and none in Aug-Sep 2025 does. D4 shows it in Mar and Aug 2026 next to the neighbour. D3 shows it blended with the neighbour in Mar 2026, fainter in Aug 2026. D2 shows nothing visible in any visit.

pixels.summary:
From the pixels and the instrument, B is a real point source at one fixed place on the sky. It was absent in Aug-Sep 2025, appeared by Feb 2026 and reached about 1.1 Jy at 4.4-5.0 um in Aug 2026. Detectors D3, D4, D5 and D6 all show it, the detectors that share an exposure agree, and its spectrum is a smooth thermal continuum (about 567 K in Aug 2026). Across 93 bright exposures it holds its sky place to about 0.25 arcsec. Over those exposures it lands anywhere on the arrays, and the detector is rotated 180 degrees between Mar and Aug 2026. Aug 2025 and Aug 2026 have identical pointing geometry, yet the source is absent in one and bright in the other. That rules out persistence, defects and ghosts of the 85 bright stars within 0.5 degrees. Its width and roundness match field stars of the same brightness, and the pictures confirm it.

The sweep's write-up has three things wrong or overstated:
1. Its Aug 2025 values (24-39 mJy) and all its D3 values are neighbour light caught in a 15-arcsec aperture, mostly a catalogued W2 9.05 star 10 arcsec away. The source itself measured at most about 2 mJy in Aug 2025, so the rise is at least about 400 times, not 35. It switched on between 2025-09-15 and 2026-02-26, not 'steadily through 2025'.
2. The catalogue 'counterpart' at 3.5-4.7 arcsec is not the source. My centroid, accurate to about 0.3 arcsec, is 3.7-4.9 arcsec from every object in Gaia, 2MASS, GLIMPSE, AllWISE and CatWISE, so whatever was there before is in none of them.
3. In Aug 2026 the brightest readings are partial (OVERFLOW) reads, D4 is saturated in 7 of 18 exposures, and the Mar 2026 spectrum is not a single blackbody (the source rose about 10% per day during that visit).

Also found: the archive's sky coordinates for exposure 2026W10_1A_0572_4 D5 are off by 17 arcsec, which makes the source seem to vanish there unless corrected. Verdict for this lens: it survives, with these caveats. Whether it is already known or reported is for the other lenses.

Nothing in SIMBAD, VSX or Gaia variability lies within 33 arcsec.

archives.summary:
This lens does not kill B: no survey shows any source at its position before 2025. Two of the sweep's statements are wrong, though.

1. **The 2025 numbers belong to a different star.** The sweep's Aug-Sep 2025 readings (D6 24, D5 39, D4 38, D3 27 mJy) and its "rises steadily through 2025" are the light of a steady red star 10 arcsec away (R: 2MASS 16524412-4440318, Ks 10.66; AllWISE W2 9.07, about 40 mJy), which falls inside the 15 arcsec aperture.
   - NEOWISE saw R steady over 21 visits from 2014 to 2024.
   - A fit that measures R and the candidate separately gives R 33-54 mJy in all three SPHEREx visits. The candidate is -0.5 +- 1.1 mJy in Aug 2025 D6, so it was not there.
   - The rise starts between Aug 2025 and Feb 2026: D6 424 +- 23 mJy in Mar 2026, 1011 +- 29 mJy in Aug 2026. D3 (about 2.2 um) peaked at 40 mJy in Mar 2026 and fell to 29 mJy by Aug 2026.

2. **The counterpart the sweep named is not the progenitor.** The 2026 source sits at 253.18040, -44.67697, 3.6 to 4.9 arcsec from that faint star. Seven control stars show SPHEREx positions in this field are good to 0.1-0.9 arcsec.

**Before 2025.** Within 2.4 arcsec of the source, the catalogues and images checked show nothing:
- 2MASS (1999), GLIMPSE (2004), MIPSGAL (2006), AllWISE, VVV and VIRAC2 (2010-2019), Deep GLIMPSE (2012), APOGLIMPSE (2017).
- NEOWISE single exposures from 2014 to March 2024 (279 detections, none at the place).
- Gaia, DECaPS images, MSX, AKARI, IRAS, Hi-GAL, ATLASGAL.
- SIMBAD, VSX and Gaia variability have nothing within 33 arcsec.

The nearest listed object is a very faint star 2.5 arcsec away (Ks 17.13, [4.5] 0.21 mJy).

**Upper limits on what was there:**

| Wavelength | Survey, year | Brightest it can have been |
|---|---|---|
| 4.5 um | Spitzer, 2004 and 2012 | under 0.7 mJy (3 sigma) |
| 4.6 um | NEOWISE, March 2024 | 1.4 mJy or less |
| about 2.2 um | VVV, 2010-2019 | under about 0.1 mJy |
| 24 um | MIPSGAL, 2006 | under 3-9 mJy |

**How much it brightened:**
- At least 300 times at 4.4-5.0 um within one year (Aug 2025 to Aug 2026, SPHEREx alone).
- At least 700 times against March 2024.
- At least 1,400 times against Spitzer in 2004 and 2012.
- At least 400 times at about 2.2 um against VVV.

**Context, not an identification.** The place is in a star-forming complex: a SPICY young-star group (G341.1-0.3), dark clouds, sub-mm clumps and a methanol maser within a few arcmin. The source got redder from Mar to Aug 2026.

Verdict: survives with caveats. Its 2025 numbers and its counterpart must be corrected. The VVV limit is inferred from the faintest stars listed, not measured. Several catalogues could not be checked because CDS was down and some mirror answers failed their controls. I did not check whether the source has already been reported (TNS, ATel, literature); that is outside this lens.

The relayed user message ("why is this keeping on changing, it is not even visible") seems to be about the app's display; this check did not touch the app or the repository.

reports.summary:
I found no previous report or catalogue entry for B in any search I could run. Most of the main channels were run with a control that works.
- Transient Name Server: nothing within 60 arcsec. Controls SN 2023ixf and V462 Lup are found, so the sweep's empty answer was a real one, not an unserved request.
- CBAT confirmation page (to 2026-11-13): nothing.
- Mukai's nova list: nearest 2025-2026 nova is 15 degrees away.
- VSX (VizieR copy of 2026-10-18): nothing within 37 arcsec.
- ATel: none of the 1,217 telegram titles of 2025-2026 concerns this place.
- SPHEREx transient papers: Karambelkar et al. 2026 and the A&A paper on four young-star outbursts (Li et al. 2026) both list other positions.
- VizieR, all catalogues within 30 arcsec: no variable, young-star, transient or X-ray entry.
- Web searches on all names and notations: nothing.

Several services that sound useful cannot see this place (ZTF, Rubin/LSST brokers, KMTNet, MOA, and Gaia, which stopped alerting in January 2025). SIMBAD's mirror does not even hold the 2025 control novae. Telegram texts and ADS could not be read.

Two corrections to the sweep's write-up come from my own measurement on the cached cutouts.
1. The 'Aug 2025' fluxes are the light of a catalogued very red star 10 arcsec away (Ks 10.66, W2 9.07). The pixel at B is essentially empty then: D6 0.38 MJy/sr. It rises to 180 and then 392 MJy/sr, so the brightening is real and larger than stated.
2. The outburst's position (RA 253.18040, Dec -44.67696, scatter 0.2 arcsec over 50 exposures) is 3.6 to 4.9 arcsec from every 'counterpart' the sweep named. The progenitor may therefore be uncatalogued.

The region is rich in young stars (SPICY region G341.1-0.3), so a young-star outburst is a natural reading, but that is not established.

For this lens the source survives with caveats: not reported in any searchable list I could reach. That is a statement about these searches, not proof that nobody has reported it.

ordinary.candidate: B: RA 253.18044, Dec -44.67687 (l 341.089, b -0.416). Re-measured position RA 253.180355, Dec -44.677008, about ±0.3 arcsec. That is 0.55 arcsec from the sweep's position.
ordinary.lens: Ordinary explanations, and what B probably is. Covered: Solar System body; known variable or eruptive object near the position; glare, spike or ghost of a bright star; physical classification; whether the rise is real in every detector.

findings.what: The sweep's August 2025 fluxes (D6 24, D5 39, D4 38, D3 27 mJy) and its picture of a source that 'rises steadily through 2025' are wrong. Those numbers are the light of a steady red star 10 arcsec to the north-east (WISEA J165244.11-444031.8 = 2MASS J16524412-4440318, W2 9.07, Ks 10.66), which sits inside the sweep's 15.4 arcsec measuring circle. I fitted the PSF at B's position with that star and four other neighbours modelled separately. B is not detected in August to September 2025 in any detector. The real change is from nothing to about 1 Jy between September 2025 and March 2026, larger than the sweep's ratio of 35.
findings.evidence: My forced PSF fluxes at B's position, Aug-Sep 2025, weighted mean ± 1σ: D6 -0.75±1.59 (12 exposures, 3σ limit 4.0 mJy), D5 -1.33±1.72 (19, limit 3.8), D4 +0.26±1.10 (11, limit 3.6), D3 -0.53±0.82 (2, limit 1.9), D2 -0.16±0.29 (9, limit 0.7). The fitted neighbour in the same fits: 31-49 mJy in D4-D6, steady in all three visits. NEOWISE measured that neighbour at W2 9.05-9.12 in all 21 visits from 2014 to 2024 (data/neowise_20as.tbl). Files: out/astro2.json, scripts/astro2.py.

findings.what: The faint catalogued star that the sweep calls B's counterpart (2MASS J16524373-4440366, Gaia DR3 5964332607636528768, GLIMPSE G341.0893-00.4165, CatWISE J165243.63) is not B. It lies about 4.5-5 arcsec east of B's measured position, about 15 times the position uncertainty. No catalogued source sits at B's position: B had no known progenitor.
findings.evidence: Position from 103 exposures in D4-D6 in March and August 2026, each corrected with 2MASS reference stars. Offset from the sweep position: E -0.21, N -0.51 arcsec. Scatter per exposure 0.12-0.23 arcsec. Control: 12 stars of Ks 9-11 fitted the same way. The 10 isolated ones land 0.13-0.60 arcsec (median 0.28) from their 2MASS positions; 2 blended pairs are off by 2-3 arcsec. Offsets from B: 2MASS/Gaia star +4.8E +0.6N; GLIMPSE +4.5E; CatWISE +3.7E. Nearest VVV DR2 source: Ks 17.33 at 2.4 arcsec, nothing brighter within 2.5 arcsec. The only GLIMPSE source within 3.7 arcsec is a 3.6 µm-only detection of 14.24 mag. Nothing in MIPSGAL within 10 arcsec, AKARI or MSX within 30, IRAS within 60; each catalogue's control returned rows. Files: out/astro_points.json, out/astro2.json, out/B_positions.png, data/viz_ir_pos.json.

findings.what: 'Not already reported' cannot be firmly claimed. TNS does not hold Galactic novae, the SIMBAD copy I could reach is at least a year out of date, and the ATel search did not run. VSX, the one check with a current control, is empty.
findings.evidence: TNS coordinate search, 120 arcsec: empty. Its control found SN 2023ixf, but the known 2025 nova V7994 Sgr is not in TNS at all. SIMBAD at CDS answered HTTP 404, so I used the CfA mirror (data/simbad_180.tsv). That mirror does not know V7994 Sgr or V691 Ser by name but does know V1716 Sco (2023). AAVSO VSX: nothing within 37 arcsec; its control found V7994 Sgr at 0 arcsec. ATel: every keyword query returned the same front page, so no search took place. Web search on the coordinates: nothing. Karambelkar et al. 2026 (arXiv 2602.07129) covers only NEOWISE-era transients, and none of them is at B.

findings.what: Not a Solar System body. JPL lists no known body near B at any visit date, and B sits at the same place on the sky five months apart.
findings.evidence: JPL sb_ident, geocentre (code 500), 6x6 arcmin field, two-pass, 6 dates: 2025-08-19 (middle of visit 1), 2026-03-07 (middle of visit 2), 2026-08-17 (middle of visit 3), 2026-08-12 13:41 (brightest D6 exposure, 1260 mJy), 2025-08-02 and 2025-09-15. All answered 'no matching records' except 2025-08-02, which returned (2018 TO63), V 23.3, at 38.6 arcsec. That return shows the same request does find known bodies. Position by detector, March vs August 2026 (E, N arcsec): D6 (-0.24,-0.42) vs (-0.30,-0.66); D5 (-0.27,-0.65) vs (-0.18,-0.52); D4 (-0.06,-0.26) vs (-0.25,-0.51). The shift is at most 0.25 arcsec. Files: data/sbident_*.json, out/sbident.log.

findings.what: No catalogued variable, long-period variable, OH/IR star, maser, young stellar object, planetary nebula, symbiotic star, R CrB star or X-ray source within 33 arcsec. Nothing listed within 1 arcmin can be B at a 0.3 arcsec position.
findings.evidence: Within 60 arcsec: SPICY 43146 = 2MASS J16524039-4440242 (Class III young-star candidate) at 33.3 arcsec; Gaia DR3 5964332646302546560 (RRc, G 19.1-19.7) at 37 arcsec; Gaia DR3 5964332543223328000 (VSX type L, G 15.5-15.8) at 58 arcsec. Further out: a molecular-cloud fragment ([DCU2021] SDG G341.088-0.3979) at 64 arcsec; SPICY candidates from 98 arcsec; Hi-GAL clump at 147 arcsec; IR dark cloud SDC G341.128-0.422 at 147; ATLASGAL clump at 154; OH 341.117-00.383 (OH/IR star) at 157 arcsec. Empty within 60 arcsec: Robitaille 2008 red sources, Marton 2016 WISE young stars, Contreras Peña 2017 VVV high-amplitude variables, Chen 2018 WISE variables, OGLE Miras (Iwanek 2022), Engels & Bunzel OH masers, MMB methanol masers, HOPS water masers, RMS, ATLASGAL, Strasbourg-ESO PNe, Belczynski symbiotics, Tisserand 2020 R CrB stars, 2SXPS, 4XMM-DR13, CSC 2.0/2.1, 2RXS, 1RXS, RASS-FSC, eRASS1. INTEGRAL/IBIS and Swift-BAT 105-month: empty within 10 arcmin. Gaia DR3 vari_summary and VSX copy dated 2026-10-18: only the RRc and the LPV. Every empty catalogue passed a control. Exception: Marton 2019 (II/360), whose control could not fetch a first row. Files: data/viz_yso_var.json, data/viz_maser_pn_x.json, out/viz_controls.txt, data/vsx_api_sep.txt.

findings.what: Not a mid-infrared variable that was there before: nothing was ever seen at B's position from 2014 to March 2024, while the 41 mJy neighbour 10 arcsec away was detected in every frame. A Mira or OH/IR star is always in AllWISE at 4.6 µm and varies by 2-6 times. B was below about 1 mJy there and then rose more than 250 times, so that class is excluded.
findings.evidence: NEOWISE-R single exposures within 20 arcsec: 561 rows, 21 visits from 2014-03-10 to 2024-03-08. Neighbour: 11-24 detections per visit, W2 median 9.05-9.12. Within 3 arcsec of B: 0 detections in all visits. AllWISE and CatWISE: nearest source to B is the 3.7-4.8 arcsec star above, W2 13.54 (0.66 mJy).

findings.what: Glare, spike or ghost of a bright star is not supported by the sky. The nearest star brighter than W2 = 4 or K = 4 is 5-9 arcmin away. The source is point-like and stays at one sky position across exposures, detectors and two visits whose spacecraft orientations differ, which an optical ghost does not do. The detector geometry itself is the pixel lens's job.
findings.evidence: Within 30 arcmin. 2MASS J16523780-4445419 (Ks 3.62, quality flag D, unreliable) at 310 arcsec, position angle 191°. AllWISE J165331.42-444215.9 (W2 3.44) at 523 arcsec, PA 101°. J165304.11-443202.6 (W2 3.78) at 561 arcsec, PA 23°. J165147.45-443429.0 (W2 3.38) at 701 arcsec. J165127.44-445055.9 (W2 0.93) at 1017 arcsec, PA 232°. J165333.68-442144.6 (W2 1.40) at 1254 arcsec, PA 25.5°. J165224.64-441253.1 (W2 -0.88, Ks 2.28) at 1676 arcsec, PA 353°. The query's control found Antares. Image width relative to field stars: D5 1.09x, D6 1.04x. Field-star calibration of each exposure (24 stars) agrees to 2-9 per cent. Files: out/bright_stars.txt, out/field_calib.json.

findings.what: The rise is real at 1.7-5 µm, and the colour changes smoothly with wavelength. A calibration error in one detector would not do this. Between March and August 2026 the H band faded, K stayed flat, 3 µm rose about 6 times, 3.9-4.2 µm about 4.7 times and 4.4-5.0 µm about 2.5 times. Within March the 4.9 µm flux rose 1.5 times in 8 days. The detectors were read on different days of a rising source (D4 Feb 26 to Mar 2, D5 Mar 4-13, D6 Mar 8-16), which accounts for the step in ratio between D4 and D5.
findings.evidence: My calibrated PSF fluxes, March then August 2026 (mJy). 2.27 µm 64.9 → 2.40 µm 57.2. 3.06 µm 26.5 → 154. D5 3.87-4.22 median 145 → 677. D6 median about 410 → 1015. H band at 1.50-1.62 µm 1.5-3.7 → about 0 (within ±1). Rates: 4.9 µm -1.83 mag/month (Mar 8-16); 4.4-5.0 µm -0.20 mag/month (Mar to Aug); 3.9-4.2 µm -0.32; 3 µm -0.33; K +0.03 (flat); H fading by more than +0.18. From the August 2025 limit (<5 mJy) to 285 mJy on 2026-03-08: brighter by more than 4.4 mag. Files: out/spectra_points.json, out/B_spectra_by_epoch.png, scripts/rates.py.

findings.what: The spectrum (each SPHEREx exposure gives one wavelength) shows the kind of object. In March 2026 it has hydrogen emission: Paschen-alpha and Brackett-alpha. In August 2026 it shows CO2-ice absorption at 4.25-4.26 µm, and in March a broad dip at 2.5-3.4 µm consistent with water ice at 3.05 µm. The August continuum is warm dust, a 575 K blackbody with no extinction or 760-860 K behind A_K 3-4. Field stars in the same exposures show no such features.
findings.evidence: March, 1.889 µm channel (holds Pa-alpha at 1.875): 43.7 mJy against 17.0 and 21.9 in the neighbouring channels, same day. March, 4.039 µm channel (holds Br-alpha at 4.052): 290.6 against 176.7 and 196.8, same day (Mar 7); the field-star correction there is 0.978. August, 4.251 and 4.260 µm: 525 and 541 against 681-734 (4.215/4.224) and 670-744 (4.287/4.296), same dates. March D4 2.54-3.41 µm: 26-39, against 56 at 2.47 and 63-76 at 3.66-3.76. Blackbody fits, August, 2.2-5.0 µm: T = 575±7 K with no extinction (reduced χ² 1.0); 687 K (A_K 2); 763 K (A_K 3); 859 K (A_K 4). March, 3.8-5.0 µm: 440-524 K, poor fit (reduced χ² 6-15). The March fit is biased by the rise during the visit and is not evidence that the dust warmed. The extinction law (Indebetouw 2005 ratios) is from memory, not re-read in this session. Files: out/sedfit.json, scripts/sedfit.py.

findings.what: Ranked reading: (1) an embedded young star in an accretion outburst; (2) a dust-forming classical nova behind heavy extinction; (3) a luminous red nova (stellar merger). Excluded: microlensing, a Mira, OH/IR or dusty giant, an R CrB star, a symbiotic star with a visible giant, and an X-ray-binary jet. Decisive observation: a 1-2.5 µm spectrum at R of 2000 or more. The source is K about 10 mag in 2026, easy for a 4-8 m telescope. Broad H I and He I lines (≥1000 km/s) would mean a nova. Narrow Br-gamma, a CO 2.29 µm bandhead (in emission or absorption) and/or H2 shock lines would mean a young star. CO and water-vapour absorption of a 2000-3000 K photosphere would mean a merger.
findings.evidence: For (1), from published examples I read. J064722.95+031644.6: W2 rose more than 500 times (more than 100 times within 2017); outburst temperature 600-700 K; quiescent K 17.35; 400-4650 Lsun at 3.5 kpc; H2 lines only (arXiv 2309.11016). WISEA J142238.82-611553.7: about 8 mag at 4.6 µm, found in an IR dark cloud, 800-1000 K (Lucas+ 2020). FU Ori-type objects in SPHEREx show H2O and CO2 ice absorption and no emission lines at SPHEREx resolution (Karambelkar+ 2026). Classical FU Ori outbursts reach 100-300 Lsun and rise in about a year; EX Lup 2008 rose 5 mag in V within 3-4 weeks (Audard+ 2014). For B, the near-by IR dark cloud and clumps and the ices favour (1); the Br-alpha/Pa-alpha emission and the less-than-6-month rise point to the EXor end. For (2): dust in V5668 Sgr condensed by day 82 at about 1090 K and was 720 K by day 113; V339 Del's dust started at about day 35 at 1480 K and peaked in mass near day 100. Against (2): novae seen by SPHEREx are 'dominated by strong emission lines' with a strong 4.5 µm feature (Mg II, C I, Al IX), which B lacks. For (3): V1309 Sco faded about 10 mag in the optical, stayed bright in the IR, had 460 K dust in 2010, and its central star was 3000-3300 K. Excluded: microlensing because the colour changed strongly; dusty giants and R CrB because there was no 4.6 µm progenitor brighter than about 1 mJy in 2004-2024; symbiotics because nothing brighter than Ks 17.3 is within 2.5 arcsec in VVV; an XRB jet because the spectrum is a curved thermal one, not a power law.

ordinary.could_not_check:
ATel: no working search. SIMBAD at CDS: down. The CfA mirror lags by at least a year, so a 2026 report would not be in it. TNS does not contain Galactic novae. So 'already reported' rests mainly on VSX, a web search and the coordinate search.
Not searched: VVV variability tables (VIVA, VVV-WIT), DREAMS, PRIME or WINTER/Gattini alerts, MAXI or Swift transients in 2025-26, Gaia DR3 YSO lists other than the Gaia/AllWISE crossmatch II/360 (whose control failed).
NEOWISE: catalogue detections only. I did not do forced photometry on the NEOWISE images, so the pre-2024 limit at B is 'never detected', not a number.
The emission lines rest on single SPHEREx channels taken on different days of a rising source. The ice identifications are a 2-channel and a 9-channel dip. None is resolved.
The extinction-law ratios (Indebetouw 2005) are from memory, not re-read. I did not derive extinction from the line ratio because I did not look up the Case B ratios.
The March 2026 temperature is unreliable because the source rose during the visit. D4 exposures at 3.3-3.8 µm in August are saturated and were excluded.
The detector geometry of ghosts (other lens): I checked only the sky geometry and position stability.
Distance: unknown. Luminosities are given for 3, 8 and 12 kpc as asked.

ordinary.summary:
On the ordinary explanations, B survives with caveats. It is not a known Solar System body, not a catalogued variable or other known object, and not a sky-geometry ghost. Two of the sweep's statements are wrong, though.

1. **B was not there in August 2025.** The sweep's August 2025 fluxes and its 'rises steadily through 2025' come from a steady W2 9.07 star 10 arcsec away, inside its 15-arcsec circle. NEOWISE shows that star constant from 2014 to 2024. With that star fitted out, B is absent in August-September 2025 (3σ limits: <4 mJy at 4.4-5.0 µm, <2 mJy at 1.7-2.4 µm). It then rose to about 285 mJy at 4.6 µm by 8 March 2026, about 430 by mid-March and about 1000 by August 2026.
2. **The 'faint counterpart' is not B.** I measured B's position to about 0.3 arcsec, checked against 2MASS control stars. The star the sweep matched lies 4.5-5 arcsec east. Nothing is catalogued at B's position: VVV has nothing brighter than Ks 17.3 within 2.5 arcsec, and NEOWISE saw nothing within 3 arcsec in 21 visits up to March 2024. So B has no known progenitor.

**Ordinary explanations ruled out:**
- *Solar System body.* JPL lists no known body near B at any visit date or at the brightest exposure; the same request did return a V 23.3 asteroid 39 arcsec away on 2 August 2025. B also stays at the same sky position to within 0.25 arcsec between March and August 2026.
- *Known object.* Nothing in about 40 catalogues within 33 arcsec (variables, young stars, masers, nebulae, X-ray sources), each checked with a control.
- *Glare or ghost.* The nearest star brighter than W2 = 4 is 8.7 arcmin away. B is point-like and holds one sky position across 103 exposures in two visits.

**The change is real.** It shows in all detectors from 1.7 to 5 µm, and the colour shifts smoothly with wavelength. Field stars in the same exposures stay within 2-9 per cent.

**What kind of object.** In August 2026 the light is warm dust: 575 K with no extinction, 760-860 K behind A_K = 3-4. That is 280-1100 Lsun at 3 kpc and 2000-7900 Lsun at 8 kpc. March 2026 shows hydrogen emission (Pa-alpha and Br-alpha). August shows CO2-ice absorption at 4.25 µm, and March shows a likely water-ice dip at 3 µm. Clumps and an IR dark cloud lie 1-2.5 arcmin away. My ranking:
1. An embedded young star in an accretion outburst. Published cases of this size exist: J0647+0316 rose more than 500 times at 4.6 µm with 600-700 K dust and a Ks 17.35 progenitor; WISEA J1422-6115 rose about 8 mag.
2. A dust-forming classical nova behind heavy extinction. Against it: novae seen by SPHEREx are dominated by strong emission lines, which B lacks.
3. A luminous red nova (stellar merger).

**Excluded classes:** microlensing, Miras and OH/IR stars, R CrB stars, symbiotic stars, and X-ray-binary jets.

**The deciding observation** is a 1-2.5 µm spectrum at R ≥ 2000; B is K about 10 mag. Broad hydrogen and helium lines would mean a nova. Narrow Br-gamma with CO bandhead and/or H2 lines would mean a young star. Cool-photosphere CO and water absorption would mean a merger.

**Caveat on 'not reported':** this is not secure. TNS does not hold Galactic novae, the SIMBAD copy I could reach lags by a year or more, and the ATel search did not work.

Separately, the user's latest message ('WHY IS THIS KEEPING ON CHANGING, IT IS NOT EVEN VISIBLE') seems to be about the app's display, which this check does not cover.
